pages.title: Restaurant prime cost: what to count and compare
pages.heading: Prime cost is a starting point. Find the reason it moved.
pages.description: How to calculate restaurant prime cost, align food and labor records, and investigate a change before adjusting staffing or purchasing.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.takeaway: Use the same reporting period for cost of goods sold, labor and sales. Then investigate the change in each component.

sections.title: The calculation
sections.body: Restaurant prime cost combines cost of goods sold with total labor cost for a defined period. Divide that total by sales for the same period and multiply by 100 to express it as a percentage. It brings two major operating costs into one view; it does not tell you the restaurant’s final profit.
items: Prime cost = cost of goods sold + total labor cost
Prime cost percentage = prime cost ÷ sales × 100
Rent, financing and other expenses still matter when assessing profitability.

sections.title: Agree what belongs in the numbers
sections.body: Confirm the accounts included with the person preparing your reports. Labor should reflect the agreed full employment-cost basis, rather than wages alone. Food and beverage cost needs a consistent inventory and purchasing basis. Document the treatment of transfers, credits and missing invoices so next week’s comparison means the same thing.

sections.title: Check the dates before the percentage
sections.body: A delivery recorded in one week and counted in another can change the picture. So can payroll covering a different number of days from the sales report. Write the period on the review, note any estimates and mark incomplete records. Resolve a cutoff difference before presenting it as an operating problem.

sections.title: Separate the two questions
sections.body: If the percentage rises, look at food and labor separately. Did sales fall while staffing stayed steady? Did a supplier’s unit price change? Was stock counted differently? Use the underlying records and the manager’s account of the week to choose the next check. A single combined percentage cannot answer those questions.
items: Food: quantities, unit prices, counts, waste and sales mix.
Labor: recorded hours, approved rates, trading hours and service context.
Sales: comparable days and a consistent reporting basis.

sections.title: Choose a target for your restaurant
sections.body: Service style, menu, hours and staffing needs affect the operating model. Agree a working target from your own records and plans, then review the reasons for a difference. Ready Margin can help connect food-cost review, labor records and reporting within the scope agreed for your restaurant.

pages.title: Restaurant month-end close checklist
pages.heading: Close the month without reopening every question.
pages.description: A restaurant month-end close checklist covering sales settlements, bank reconciliation, supplier bills, payroll records and unresolved items.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.takeaway: A close checklist needs source records, responsible people and an explicit list of what remains unresolved.

sections.title: Put a date and a person against each job
sections.body: Start with the reporting period, the intended close date and the person responsible for each input. A checklist that says only ‘payroll’ or ‘bank’ leaves too much open. State which record is needed, where it comes from and who can answer a difference. Confirm the review date with the person who will use the reports.

sections.title: Match sales to the way money arrives
sections.body: Gather POS summaries, settlement statements, delivery-platform statements and bank activity. Reconcile receipts to their source, keeping fees, refunds and timing differences visible. A deposit landing after month-end is a question of timing to confirm, not automatically a missing sale.
items: Identify the sales and settlement dates.
Separate fees, refunds and other statement adjustments.
Record unexplained differences for investigation.

sections.title: Check the costs that tend to arrive late
sections.body: Review supplier bills against deliveries and known commitments. Ask about missing invoices and credits. Confirm payroll records and any outstanding corrections. Your accountant should agree the treatment of costs belonging to the month when the final document has not arrived. Keep that decision with the working papers.

sections.title: Reconcile and review
sections.body: Compare bank and card accounts to their statements, investigate outstanding items and review unusual balances. Where inventory is included, confirm the count date and any transfers. Check that account and location mapping is consistent before comparing the results with a prior period or another restaurant.

sections.title: Send the explanation with the statements
sections.body: The handoff should include the agreed financial statements, what changed, and the questions still open. Each open item needs an owner and next check. A report marked provisional is more useful than a report that quietly leaves out uncertainty. Ready Margin’s accounting and close service agrees these responsibilities during onboarding.
items: Completed reconciliations and supporting records.
Material changes with operating context.
Outstanding items, assigned people and follow-up dates.

pages.title: Restaurant recipe costing and portion review
pages.heading: Does the recipe cost match what leaves the kitchen?
pages.description: A practical restaurant recipe-costing review: current supplier prices, pack sizes, usable yield, portion size and the limits of dish-margin calculations.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant recipe costing and dish margin
pages.takeaway: Keep the purchase unit, usable yield and serving size consistent before comparing a dish’s ingredient cost with its selling price.

sections.title: Start with the recipe you actually serve
sections.body: Confirm ingredients, preparation method and portion size with the kitchen. Include sauces, garnishes and components prepared in batches. A recipe written for a previous menu or a different portion will produce a precise answer to the wrong question. Give the working recipe a date and record who checked it.

sections.title: Make the units comparable
sections.body: A case price cannot go straight into a recipe that uses ounces or grams. Record the pack size, convert to a consistent unit and allow for usable yield where trimming or preparation changes the quantity available. Check supplier substitutions: a familiar item name does not guarantee an unchanged pack.
items: Confirm the latest invoice price and pack quantity.
Convert purchase units to recipe units.
Record yield assumptions and the portion served.

sections.title: Build from ingredient to portion
sections.body: Multiply each ingredient’s usable unit cost by the quantity used. Add the ingredients to establish batch cost, then divide by the usable portions the batch produces. Keep the calculation close to the source invoice and recipe so someone else can repeat it when a price or portion changes.

sections.title: Ingredient margin is not the whole profit
sections.body: The selling price less ingredient cost can help compare menu items, but it still has to support labor and other operating costs. Sales mix matters too: the dish with an attractive ingredient margin may not be a popular order. Read costing alongside the menu’s actual sales and the work required to prepare it.

sections.title: Pick one change to investigate
sections.body: When a cost looks wrong, check the inputs before changing the menu. The useful next step might be a pack-size check, a recipe update or an observed portion review. Ready Margin can support recipe and supplier-cost analysis; your team confirms what happens in the kitchen and decides which changes to make.

pages.title: Restaurant bookkeeper, CPA or fractional CFO?
pages.heading: Choose support for the work you need done.
pages.description: Compare restaurant bookkeeping, CPA and fractional CFO responsibilities, then identify who owns the records, interpretation and follow-through.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant bookkeeper vs CPA vs fractional CFO
pages.takeaway: Job titles are a starting point. Ask for the actual deliverables, cadence, approvals and boundaries in writing.

sections.title: First, name the gap
sections.body: Are the books behind, the reports hard to use, or decisions piling up despite having both? Those are different problems. Write down one recent example and identify where the work stopped. The answer may call for a clearer handoff between existing providers, additional recurring support, or a more involved advisory relationship.

sections.title: Bookkeeping keeps the records moving
sections.body: A bookkeeping engagement commonly covers recording transactions, maintaining accounts and reconciling activity. Restaurant work can also involve sales settlements, supplier bills and payroll records. Confirm whether close support, reporting and exception follow-up are included. Do not assume that recording a transaction includes investigating every operational question behind it.

sections.title: A CPA’s scope depends on the engagement
sections.body: A CPA may provide tax, accounting or assurance services, depending on the firm and the agreed work. That title does not tell you whether someone is checking missing time entries during the week or following up on a supplier credit. Ask which responsibilities the engagement covers and which require your team or another provider.

sections.title: CFO-level guidance helps work through decisions
sections.body: An advisory relationship can help interpret the numbers, examine cash commitments, compare options and review a plan. Its usefulness depends on the quality and timing of the underlying records. If the records need recurring work, agree who does it; otherwise the review can become another meeting spent establishing the facts.

sections.title: Ask how the relationship will work
sections.body: Ready Margin combines agreed restaurant finance and operating work with explanation and practical guidance. The proposal should make the responsibilities explicit, including any specialist work handled separately. Bring the same questions to every provider so you can compare the service rather than the title.
items: Which jobs will you own, and which remain with us?
What arrives each week or month?
Who investigates missing or conflicting records?
Who approves payments, payroll and changes?
What happens when a question falls outside the engagement?

pages.title: Restaurant delivery-platform reconciliation
pages.heading: The delivery sales total isn’t the bank deposit.
pages.description: How to review restaurant delivery-platform settlements against sales, fees, refunds, adjustments and the deposit that reaches the bank.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.takeaway: Reconcile each settlement to its source period and adjustments before comparing it with a bank deposit.

sections.title: Use the settlement as the bridge
sections.body: A sales export describes activity. A platform statement explains how that activity becomes a payout. A bank statement shows when the payout arrived. Keep all three together. Comparing gross sales directly with a deposit skips the fees, refunds, adjustments and timing that may account for the difference.

sections.title: Match the location and period
sections.body: Confirm which restaurant, account and order dates the payout covers. Check whether a settlement spans two reporting periods or whether one bank deposit combines several settlements. Keep identifiers with the record so the next person can trace the match without reconstructing your work.
items: Restaurant or location identifier.
Statement period and payout reference.
Expected and actual settlement date.

sections.title: Read each adjustment
sections.body: Separate the items shown on the platform statement instead of treating the net difference as one expense. Fees, refunds, promotions and other adjustments may need different treatment. Confirm that treatment with whoever maintains the accounts and document anything whose meaning is unclear.

sections.title: Keep a short exceptions list
sections.body: Record missing statements, unmatched deposits and unexplained deductions. Include the amount from the source record, the question, the person investigating and the next check date. Preserve the original statement when requesting clarification so a correction can be followed back to the relevant payout.

sections.title: Bring it into the weekly review
sections.body: Settlement questions belong beside the cash view and the close checklist. The aim is to understand what has arrived, what is pending and what needs an answer. Ready Margin can review the required records and access during onboarding; this does not imply a direct integration with any particular delivery platform.

pages.title: Restaurant compliance records and handoffs
pages.heading: A due date needs someone responsible for it.
pages.description: Organize restaurant compliance handoffs with confirmed requirements, source documents, internal cutoffs, approvers and a record of completion.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant compliance calendar and document handoff
pages.takeaway: A working calendar connects each confirmed obligation to its records, preparer, approver and completion evidence.

sections.title: Confirm the requirement before adding the reminder
sections.body: Requirements depend on the business, location and activity. Start with the obligations confirmed for your restaurant by the appropriate authority or qualified adviser. A generic checklist cannot establish everything that applies. This guide describes how to organize the work after those requirements are confirmed; it does not set filing dates or interpret the law.

sections.title: Give each obligation a complete entry
sections.body: The calendar should explain what must be prepared and who is responsible, not just when a reminder appears. Include an internal cutoff that leaves time to obtain missing records and review the work before the confirmed external deadline. Keep the source of the requirement with the entry so it can be checked when circumstances change.
items: Requirement and the source used to confirm it.
Responsible preparer and nominated approver.
Required records and agreed secure sharing route.
Internal cutoff, confirmed deadline and escalation contact.

sections.title: Keep documents with the handoff
sections.body: A preparer should be able to see which version was approved, what remains missing and who can answer a question. Keep access limited to the people who need the records. Employee and financial documents belong in the agreed secure process, not in the public website enquiry form.

sections.title: Record completion, then the next check
sections.body: A reminder marked done is not the same as evidence that the required action was completed. Keep the relevant confirmation or receipt and note who checked it. If the work is still outstanding, make that status explicit and use the escalation route agreed for the restaurant.

sections.title: Agree what Ready Margin handles
sections.body: Compliance and tax-related workflows are agreed as part of the service scope, including the documents, responsible people and approvals involved. Confirm any filing or specialist work separately. The restaurant’s obligations do not disappear when a supporting workflow is outsourced; the relationship should make the responsibilities easier to follow.

pages.title: Restaurant payroll services: what the handoff should make clear
pages.seoTitle: Restaurant Payroll Services | Hours, Tips & Approval Handoffs

pages.takeaway: A reliable payroll handoff names the period, the records, the approver and the route for exceptions before the deadline is close.

sections.title: Start before payroll day
sections.body: Payroll is easier to check when the team has agreed the pay period and internal cutoff before managers are pressed for answers. Put the dates, source records and one person responsible for collecting questions in the same place. A request for a last-minute correction should be visible as an exception, not buried in a message thread.
items: Pay-period dates and internal cutoff.
Source of time, absence and tip records.
Named manager for questions and corrections.

sections.title: Match recorded time with the operating week
sections.body: A time entry by itself rarely explains a difference. Compare the relevant schedule, recorded hours and manager context for the same shift. A changed trade period, a missed punch and an approved cover shift may look similar in a report but need different records. Keep the explanation with the correction so it can be traced at the next review.

sections.title: Keep tip inputs clear
sections.body: Tip data should follow the restaurant’s documented policy and the agreed payroll process. Confirm the period, the source of the figures and who has checked unusual amounts before the data is prepared for approval. Employment, tax and jurisdiction-specific advice remain with the appropriate adviser unless that work is specifically confirmed in scope.

sections.title: Preparation is not approval
sections.body: A support team can prepare the records, list the questions and make the handoff easier to review. The restaurant’s nominated approver still decides whether payroll is ready to run. Keeping those roles separate protects the decision trail and makes it clear where an unresolved item needs to go.
items: Prepared inputs and a record of changes.
A concise list of open questions.
An explicit approval point before the run.

sections.title: Agree the exception route
sections.body: Late changes happen. The useful question is not whether they can be eliminated, but how they are recorded and who decides what to do. Agree the cutoff, escalation contact and treatment for a correction that arrives after approval. Ready Margin’s payroll and tips support is scoped around these working handoffs rather than a generic package.

pages.title: Restaurant bookkeeping services: what reliable records need each week
pages.seoTitle: Restaurant Bookkeeping Services | Reconciliation & Monthly Close
pages.heading: A close cannot rescue a month of missing handoffs.
pages.description: What restaurant bookkeeping services should keep moving each week: sales settlements, bills, account reconciliation and a clear route for unresolved records.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant bookkeeping services, restaurant accounting support, outsourced restaurant bookkeeping
pages.takeaway: Reliable restaurant bookkeeping depends on timely source records, consistent treatment and an open-item list that does not disappear at month-end.

sections.title: The records arrive in fragments
sections.body: Restaurant bookkeeping has to bring together more than a bank feed. Sales settlements, delivery statements, supplier bills, card activity, payroll records and approvals can all arrive on different dates. Decide how each record reaches the work file and who can answer a missing or unclear item. The aim is not a perfect inbox; it is a dependable route for getting the right record to the right review.

sections.title: Keep sales, settlements and cash distinct
sections.body: A sales report describes trading activity. A settlement shows how a provider processed that activity. A deposit shows when cash reached the account. Keep those records connected without treating them as identical. When the dates differ, record the timing difference and investigate anything that cannot be explained from the source documents.
items: Sales and settlement period.
Payout reference and bank date.
Fees, refunds, credits and unresolved differences.

sections.title: Bills need a clear status
sections.body: A supplier bill might be approved, waiting for delivery confirmation, disputed or missing. Those are different states, and each needs a named next step. A clean workflow keeps the document, the question and the approval route together so the close does not turn into a search for context.

sections.title: Reconciliation creates a useful questions list
sections.body: Reconciling an account is not simply matching a total. It shows what has cleared, what is pending and what needs an explanation. Keep any unexplained item on a dated list with an owner. That gives the monthly close an honest starting point and avoids pretending that an unknown difference has been settled.

sections.title: Agree what the service includes
sections.body: Restaurant bookkeeping can include recurring recording, reconciliations, close preparation and reporting support, but the exact work depends on the records, systems and approval structure already in place. Ready Margin confirms that scope in writing, including the handoffs that remain with the restaurant or another adviser.

pages.title: Restaurant cash flow management: turn a bank balance into a weekly plan
pages.seoTitle: Restaurant Cash Flow Management | Weekly Cash Visibility Support
pages.heading: A bank balance is a snapshot, not a cash plan.
pages.description: A restaurant cash-flow management guide for reviewing expected receipts, payroll, supplier commitments and timing differences before the next decision is due.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant cash flow management, restaurant cash flow support, weekly cash flow review for restaurants
pages.takeaway: A useful cash view is dated, explicit about known commitments and clear about what is estimated or still unconfirmed.

sections.title: Start with the date and the balance
sections.body: Use the current bank position as the start of a conversation, not the answer. State the date and account basis, then list the receipts and commitments expected before the next review. A balance can look comfortable while payroll, supplier payments or a delayed settlement are already spoken for.

sections.title: Separate what is known from what is assumed
sections.body: Some items are supported by an approved payment, settlement statement or agreed payroll amount. Others are estimates, timing assumptions or questions that need confirmation. Label them differently. That makes the cash view more useful to the person deciding what can be paid, deferred or investigated.
items: Confirmed available cash and account date.
Expected receipts with source and likely timing.
Known commitments, approval status and due date.
Estimates or unresolved items with a next check.

sections.title: Read sales in context
sections.body: A strong sales week may not produce cash in the same week. Card and delivery settlement timing, refunds, fees and outstanding invoices can change when money becomes available. Compare the operating record with the cash record before treating a sales movement as a cash answer.

sections.title: Make commitments visible before they are urgent
sections.body: Payroll, supplier bills, rent, taxes and other obligations are not interchangeable. Record the agreed due date, the approver and any question that affects timing. If a payment cannot be confirmed, make that uncertainty visible rather than allowing it to vanish into a broad cash total.

sections.title: Use the review to choose a next action
sections.body: Cash reporting is most useful when it ends with a named decision: confirm a settlement, resolve a bill, review a payment schedule or request an updated forecast. It cannot guarantee future cash. Ready Margin can provide reporting and cash-visibility support within an agreed scope, with the assumptions kept beside the numbers.

pages.title: Restaurant labor cost management: look beyond the schedule
pages.seoTitle: Restaurant Labor Cost Management | Scheduling, Time & Payroll Support
pages.heading: Before changing labor, understand the week that produced it.
pages.description: A restaurant labor-cost management guide for connecting schedules, recorded hours, pay inputs and service context before making a staffing decision.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant labor cost management, restaurant labor cost support, restaurant scheduling and payroll
pages.takeaway: A labor-cost review is more reliable when the sales period, schedule, recorded time and pay inputs describe the same operating week.

sections.title: Set the comparison before drawing a conclusion
sections.body: Choose a reporting period that makes sense for the restaurant and make sure sales, scheduled hours and recorded hours cover it consistently. A payroll period can overlap a different number of trading days than a weekly sales report. Note that mismatch before calling an increase a scheduling problem.

sections.title: Read the schedule with the time record
sections.body: A schedule tells you what was planned. The time record shows what was recorded. Manager context explains a changed shift, a cover, an early close or a service issue. Put all three together before asking why labor moved. That reduces the risk of correcting the wrong part of the operation.
items: Scheduled coverage and trading hours.
Recorded hours and approved corrections.
Service, weather, event or operating context where relevant.

sections.title: Keep pay inputs and attendance questions connected
sections.body: A missing punch, changed rate or tip input can affect the payroll handoff as well as the labor view. Record the question once, assign the person who can confirm it and make sure the resolution reaches both processes. Repeating the same correction in separate spreadsheets is where small issues become hard to trace.

sections.title: Avoid a universal target
sections.body: Restaurant format, service model, menu, hours and team structure change the labor picture. Use the restaurant’s own plan and history with comparable weeks. A percentage may highlight a question, but it cannot decide the right staffing level without the operating context.

sections.title: Turn the finding into one workable next step
sections.body: The next action might be a time-record correction, a review of a recurring shift pattern or a clearer approval rule. Ready Margin can connect scheduling, attendance and payroll preparation within the agreed service scope. Staffing, pay policy and employment decisions remain with the restaurant and its appropriate advisers.

pages.title: Why restaurant sales do not equal available cash
pages.heading: A good sales week is not the same as cash in the bank.
pages.description: How to read restaurant sales alongside settlement timing, payroll and supplier commitments before making a cash decision.

sections.title: The dining room was full. Why does cash still feel tight?
sections.body: Sales tell you what the restaurant sold. Available cash depends on when receipts settle and what is already committed. A busy week and a tight payment schedule can happen at the same time.

sections.title: Check when the money arrives
sections.body: Compare the sales period with the bank activity. Card settlements, refunds and other timing differences may explain part of the gap. Use the source records to confirm the dates before treating it as a loss.

sections.title: Put the due dates beside the balance
sections.body: List known payroll, supplier and other operating commitments. Mark anything estimated or not yet confirmed. A bank balance read on its own can make money look available when it already has a job.

sections.title: Decide what needs an answer
sections.body: Which receipt has not settled? Which bill is still missing? Who can confirm it? Give each unresolved question a person and a date, then refresh the view before making the decision.

pages.takeaway: Read the balance with settlement dates and known commitments—not on its own.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: Why restaurant sales do not equal available cash

pages.title: A calmer payroll handoff starts before cutoff
pages.heading: Payroll starts before the cutoff email.
pages.description: A restaurant payroll preparation checklist for confirming hours, tip inputs, corrections and the final approval.

sections.title: Agree the period first
sections.body: Schedules, attendance and tip inputs need to cover the same pay period. Confirm the dates before the team starts comparing records.

sections.title: Collect the exceptions in one place
sections.body: Missing clock-outs, changed shifts and incomplete tip inputs need a manager’s answer. Keep a short working list in the approved secure process, with the person responsible for each correction.

sections.title: Name the approver
sections.body: Preparing payroll and authorizing it are different jobs. Confirm who signs off and when. The person collecting corrections should know exactly where the prepared record goes.

sections.title: Check the final version
sections.body: Make sure the agreed corrections reached the submission. A resolved message is not enough if the payroll input still holds the old value. Keep an agreed route for anything that changes after cutoff.

pages.takeaway: Check that each correction reached the final record before it goes for approval.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial

pages.title: Food cost moved. Which question comes first?
pages.heading: Food cost changed. Don’t change the menu just yet.
pages.description: How restaurant operators can investigate a food-cost change by checking prices, quantities, portions and reporting periods.

sections.title: First, check the comparison
sections.body: Are you comparing the same period, product and unit? A different pack size or delivery date can change the number without changing the underlying price.

sections.title: Look at what happened in the kitchen
sections.body: Current recipes, yields, portions, stock counts and waste records help explain the result. If one of those inputs is an estimate, say so. Do not give an uncertain calculation the weight of a confirmed fact.

sections.title: Follow the most useful lead
sections.body: A supplier price change needs a different response from a count error. Pick the record most likely to explain the movement and ask the person closest to it to check.

sections.title: Bring the finding back
sections.body: Record what was confirmed and what still needs work. Use that finding to discuss an order, recipe or operating change. A percentage alone is not enough reason to cut portions or replace a supplier.

pages.takeaway: Check the records behind the change before deciding what to change in the restaurant.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: Food cost moved. Which question comes first?

pages.title: The attendance questions to settle before payroll
pages.heading: A changed shift needs a changed record.
pages.description: Restaurant attendance checks that connect schedule changes, recorded hours and manager confirmation before payroll.

sections.title: Start with the shift, not just the time entry
sections.body: Put the schedule, attendance record and manager notes together for the same period. A mismatch may be a genuine shift change rather than a timekeeping error.

sections.title: Ask someone who was there
sections.body: The manager closest to the shift can confirm the operating facts. Keep the confirmation with the correction through the agreed process so the approver can understand the change.

sections.title: Give the question a deadline
sections.body: If the answer is still missing near payroll cutoff, tell the approver what is unresolved. Name who is checking it and what happens if it remains open.

sections.title: Notice the repeat problems
sections.body: If the same corrections arrive every cycle, look at the process that creates them. A clearer shift-change routine may help more than another reminder sent at the last minute.

pages.takeaway: Keep the manager’s confirmation connected to the corrected attendance record.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: The attendance questions to settle before payroll

pages.title: A useful supplier bill review goes beyond the total
pages.heading: Before you approve the bill, check the delivery.
pages.description: A restaurant supplier invoice review covering delivery records, quantities, pack sizes, credits and price differences.

sections.title: Line up the paperwork
sections.body: Compare the invoice with the order and delivery record where available. If one is missing, treat it as a question to resolve before concluding that the supplier made an error.

sections.title: Read the units
sections.body: Check quantities and pack sizes before comparing prices. Look for substitutions, credits and changes to the order that could explain a different total.

sections.title: Get the right person involved
sections.body: The manager who received the delivery may be able to confirm a quantity or substitution. Someone with supplier responsibility can query a price. Your nominated approver still authorizes payment.

sections.title: Keep the answer for next time
sections.body: If the issue repeats, save the explanation with the vendor review. The team should not have to investigate the same pack-size change from scratch each month.

pages.takeaway: Compare the order, delivery and invoice before treating a total as a price change.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: A useful supplier bill review goes beyond the total

pages.title: Five questions for a useful weekly P&L review
pages.heading: Five questions to ask of your restaurant P&L.
pages.description: A practical weekly restaurant P&L review: check the period, missing records, cost movements, operating context and next decision.

sections.title: 1. Which period am I looking at?
sections.body: Confirm the reporting dates and comparison period. Different numbers of trading days or different reporting cutoffs can make an apparent change misleading.

sections.title: 2. What is still missing?
sections.body: Ask whether supplier bills, payroll inputs or other records are incomplete. A report can be useful before every detail is final, but you need to know its limits.

sections.title: 3. What moved?
sections.body: Identify the material change and the records supporting it. Separate a timing difference from a volume change or a cost that needs investigation.

sections.title: 4. What happened in the restaurant?
sections.body: Ask about changes in trading, staffing, purchasing or service. The operating explanation belongs beside the financial one.

sections.title: 5. What do we do with this?
sections.body: Choose the decision or the next check, name the person responsible and set the review date. If nothing is yet supported by the records, the next action may simply be to confirm a missing input.

pages.takeaway: A useful P&L review connects the period, completeness and operating context to a decision.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: Five questions for a useful weekly P&L review

sections.title: Agree the accounting basis

sections.title: Keep the restaurant in the picture

sections.title: Check who is still waiting on records
sections.body: One location’s late bill or payroll input can distort the comparison. Show what is incomplete and when it will be updated.

sections.title: Use the comparison to ask better questions
sections.body: Review an exception with the local manager. Shared reporting should support a useful discussion, not turn different operating conditions into an unexplained ranking.

pages.takeaway: Standardize the reporting basis, then explain the differences that still matter.

faqs.question: What would you take off my plate?
faqs.answer: That depends on where you need help. We can discuss accounting, payroll and tips, attendance, food cost, supplier work and reporting. Your proposal sets out the exact work and responsibilities.

faqs.question: Is this software or a service?
faqs.answer: A managed service. People handle the agreed work and review it with you. Ready Margin software is a future direction, not a product you need to purchase today.

faqs.question: Will we have to replace our systems?
faqs.answer: We start by reviewing what you already use. Access, exports and compatibility are confirmed before we agree the scope. We do not assume that a direct integration is available.

faqs.question: How much does it cost?
faqs.answer: Pricing is by enquiry. Locations, payroll complexity, systems, the condition of the records and the support you need all affect the scope. We discuss those before preparing a proposal.

faqs.question: What should I bring to the first conversation?
faqs.answer: The systems you use, who handles the recurring jobs and one recent example of work that took too much chasing. A few notes are enough. Please keep sensitive records out of the website form.
